name: St. George–North Shore
character: The free ferry terminal funnels every island commuter through a hillside civic downtown of Sri Lankan eateries and a struggling outlet mall — fabric that behaves Brooklyn-adjacent, not suburban-island.

name: Fordham–Belmont–Bedford Park
character: Fordham Road's high-volume chain retail, Arthur Avenue's destination food heritage, Fordham University and the Zoo/Botanical Garden combine into the Bronx's densest multi-anchor demand node.

name: Pelham Bay–Throggs Neck
character: Suburban-form east-Bronx belt of single-family enclaves and Crosby/Westchester Ave retail, unified by Pelham Bay Park and Orchard Beach as its shared seasonal waterfront engine.

name: Williamsburg–Greenpoint
character: Matured creative waterfront where affluent residents, destination nightlife and national-brand retail now share one walkable L/G corridor.

name: Flatbush–Midwood–Prospect-Lefferts
character: Caribbean commercial core along Flatbush Avenue with Victorian Flatbush and PLG gentrifying at the park edge and Brooklyn College anchoring Midwood.

name: Downtown Brooklyn–Fort Greene
character: Brooklyn's civic-office-transit nexus joining the Barclays arena and BAM cultural district with brownstone Fort Greene.

name: Astoria–Ditmars
character: Food-famous, subway-fed young-professional corridor whose dining/bar gravity along 30th Ave, Broadway, Ditmars and Steinway makes it behave as one evening-and-weekend object.

name: Long Island City–Hunters Point
character: Waterfront tower cluster opposite Midtown where new residential supply, office stubs and park-side retail move in lockstep off an unmatched subway/ferry/LIRR stack.

name: Murray Hill–Kips Bay
character: Post-grad apartment spine and hospital row whose steady young-professional churn supports a reliable if unglamorous bar-and-casual strip.

name: East New York–Brownsville
character: Underserved deep-residential value market anchored by the Broadway Junction transit complex with a first wave of rezoning-era development.

name: Sunset Park–Industry City
character: Working-class Latino-Asian residential belt on the 5th/8th Avenue spines, with the Industry City–Bush Terminal innovation waterfront scored separately as a special-zone host.

name: Coney Island–Brighton–Sheepshead Bay
character: Year-round Russian-Turkish residential waterfront at the end of the subway lines, with the Coney amusement district as a separate seasonal host.

name: Chelsea–Meatpacking
character: Gallery district and Meatpacking nightlife over a residential Chelsea base, with the High Line as its western spine.

name: Co-op City–Baychester
character: Towers-in-the-park superblock population of 40k-plus ringed by highways, with Bay Plaza's chain mall and Hutchinson Metro Center offices as its shared commercial heart.

name: FiDi–Battery Park
character: Office core mid-conversion to a mixed residential district, with a waterfront tourist edge that empties after market close.

name: Central & West Harlem
character: Historic Black cultural core in sustained transition, where 125th Street national retail meets brownstone restoration and rising incomes.

name: Upper West Side
character: Family brownstone-and-boulevard residential band anchored by Lincoln Center and the parks, with stable high-income demand.

name: Ridgewood
character: Walkable Brooklyn-border corridor where creative spillover momentum along the M/L meets legacy European and Latino retail on a tight prewar tenement-and-brick grid.

name: Times Square–Hell's Kitchen
character: Global tourist and theater peak sharing one grid with a dense local restaurant row, so visitor flows and neighborhood demand overlap.

name: Morningside Heights–Manhattanville
character: University-and-institution district whose demand calendar and retail mix are set by Columbia, Barnard and the growing Manhattanville campus.

name: Bed-Stuy
character: Deep-residential brownstone belt with a maturing Tompkins/Franklin restaurant scene and steady professional inflow.

name: West Village–Greenwich Village
character: Landmarked, ultra-affluent village street grid that behaves as one restaurant-and-nightlife destination with fierce indie character.

name: Carroll Gardens–Cobble Hill–Columbia Waterfront
character: Affluent brownstone restaurant district where the Smith, Court and Columbia Street spines carry chef-led dining, bakeries and boutiques for settled high-income family households.

name: Mid-Island–New Dorp
character: The island's retail core — New Dorp Lane main street, the Hylan Boulevard spine and the Staten Island Mall node — serving stable middle-class families along the SIR's middle stations.

name: Crown Heights–Prospect Heights
character: Park-and-museum-edge brownstone corridor absorbing professional inflow along the Franklin/Vanderbilt restaurant rows.

name: DUMBO–Brooklyn Heights
character: Affluent waterfront enclave where global bridge-and-promenade tourism overlays high-income residents and creative-office workers.

name: Bay Ridge
character: Stable multi-ethnic family corridor at the Verrazzano edge anchored by the strong 3rd/5th Avenue retail spines.

name: Borough Park–Kensington
character: Large Orthodox Jewish family community whose 13th Avenue kosher retail spine runs on a Shabbat rhythm — strong weekday-evening commerce, a Friday-evening-to-Saturday shutdown that zeroes Saturday trade, and a largely captive in-community supply ecology.

name: South Shore
character: NYC's most suburban belt — affluent cul-de-sac homeownership from Great Kills to Tottenville, where the car is default and retail is plazas, big boxes and Italian family restaurants.

name: Upper East Side
character: New York's archetypal affluent residential corridor, from Museum Mile culture to Yorkville's post-2nd-Ave-subway younger infill.

name: Sunnyside–Woodside
character: 7-line immigrant bedroom spine unified by Queens Boulevard and Roosevelt Avenue pubs, diners and a steady commute rhythm.

name: Concourse–Yankee Stadium–Highbridge
character: Civic-stadium spine where Yankee Stadium event surges, Bronx courthouse workday traffic and the Grand Concourse's art-deco residential stock share one transit-rich corridor.

name: Midtown East–Grand Central
character: The city's office heart and commuter funnel, stabilizing post-RTO with quiet residential pockets that vanish into the weekday tide.

name: Maspeth–Middle Village–Glendale
character: Stable Fresh Pond family belt moving to car rhythms along Metropolitan Avenue and Fresh Pond Road retail, seamed by rail yards and expressway edges.

name: Jamaica
character: A transit-hub downtown (LIRR, AirTrain, E/J/Z, bus web) whose revitalization pipeline and Jamaica Avenue value retail rise or stall together.

name: Hunts Point–Longwood
character: The region's overnight food-distribution engine on an industrial peninsula adjoining Longwood's dense residential grid — a corridor whose clock runs on market shifts, not office hours.

name: Flatiron–Gramercy–NoMad
character: Tech offices, destination restaurants and boutique hotels orbiting Madison Square Park as one polished work-live-stay district.

name: St. Albans–Cambria Heights–Laurelton–Rosedale
character: Caribbean-Black homeowner family belt along the Merrick and Linden Boulevard corridors, bus-and-LIRR-edge fed, with value retail and church-and-civic weekend rhythms.

name: Union Square–East Village
character: NYU-driven student mass layered on legacy counterculture blocks, giving the city's deepest bar-and-cheap-eats density around a transit hub.

name: Red Hook
character: Highway-and-water-isolated village of artist lofts and indie storefronts where IKEA and the waterfront parks pull weekend destination traffic into a no-subway, bus-and-ferry peninsula.

name: Howard Beach–Ozone Park
character: Stable car-led family belt of mainland south Queens from Howard Beach through Ozone Park, moving to car rhythms with the A train as its northern-edge subway spine and JFK next door as gateway context only.

name: Jackson Heights–Elmhurst–Corona
character: Some of the densest immigrant retail in America, pulsing as a single all-day street market under the 7 viaduct and along 37th/74th/82nd and Queens Boulevard.

name: Canarsie–Marine Park–Mill Basin
character: Suburban-form, car-led family Brooklyn where Kings Plaza mall and strip corridors serve stable homeowner blocks.

name: Bushwick–East Williamsburg
character: Arts-driven industrial conversion frontier whose economy is disproportionately anchored by destination nightlife venues.

name: Forest Hills–Rego Park–Kew Gardens
character: Garden-apartment affluence linking Austin Street and Queens Boulevard retail with LIRR-speed commuter habits and a stable multi-ethnic professional base.

name: Bensonhurst–Bath Beach
character: Multi-ethnic family corridor where legacy Italian retail has ceded to Chinese, Russian and Middle Eastern corridors along 86th St and 18th Ave.

name: Lower East Side–Chinatown
character: Immigrant wholesale-retail economy meeting spillover nightlife and micro-scene fashion, all on the same tenement street fabric.

name: Soundview–Parkchester–Castle Hill
character: Planned-community towers at Parkchester — a managed private retail micro-ecology — alongside Soundview and Castle Hill family blocks sharing the 6 line and Westchester/Castle Hill Ave value retail.

name: Midtown West–Penn–Herald Square
character: Commuter-and-shopper crossroads around Penn Station, Herald Square retail and Koreatown's 24-hour strip; MSG–Penn arena surges are a special-zone overlay, not scored into this corridor.

name: Queens Village–Bellerose–Floral Park
character: Car-led family Queens along the Hillside Avenue belt from Queens Village to Floral Park and Glen Oaks, tied to strip retail, parkways and high homeownership.

name: Roosevelt Island
character: Tram-and-bridge-dependent East River island whose transit-captive residents and modest Main Street retail move as one quiet node; Cornell Tech is a separate campus zone and is not scored into this corridor.

name: Stapleton–Park Hill–Clifton
character: Rezoned Bay Street waterfront (Urby, the old Homeport) meeting steep hillside immigrant enclaves — Liberian, Mexican, Sri Lankan — making this the island's most Brooklyn-like transition frontier.

name: Park Slope–Gowanus
character: Established family-brownstone spine along Prospect Park beside a mid-transformation rezoned canal district.

name: Hudson Yards
character: Still-filling mega-development with its own mall-and-office ecology, luxury towers and the Edge/Vessel tourist draw at the 7-train terminus.

name: Rockaway Peninsula
character: Barrier-island beach economy across Jamaica Bay: summer surf-and-boardwalk demand layered on a working-class year-round base, Sandy-exposed, with Arverne-by-the-Sea momentum and total dependence on the A, Cross Bay bridges and the ferry.

name: East Harlem–El Barrio
character: Latino retail spines along 116th Street and Lexington Avenue, with Second Avenue subway access pulling new investment and residents into a deep value market.

name: Morris Park–Pelham Parkway
character: Hospital-city corridor where Einstein/Jacobi/Montefiore's 24/7 medical workforce anchors a stable, immigrant-succeeding family district along Morris Park Ave and the parkway malls.

name: Washington Heights–Inwood
character: Dense Dominican residential hills anchored by the Columbia-Presbyterian medical campus, with vibrant value retail along Broadway and 181st.

name: Flushing
character: A self-contained Asian CBD and regional shopping destination anchored on the 7 terminus, Main Street and its malls, drawing all of northeast Queens daily.

name: Riverdale–Kingsbridge
character: Hill-and-parkway northwest: leafy estate-area Riverdale above dense working-class Kingsbridge along the 1 train and Broadway, with Van Cortlandt Park and the Metro-North commuter funnel; internal split recorded.

name: Mott Haven–Port Morris
character: Harlem-river waterfront where luxury tower deliveries (Bankside) and a brewery/gallery strip meet legacy NYCHA and light industry, moving as one gentrification frontier.

name: South Williamsburg
character: Hasidic enclave whose Lee Avenue retail runs on a Sabbath rhythm — strong weekday-evening trade, a Friday-sundown-to-Saturday shutdown, and largely in-community supply.

name: West Shore–Richmond Valley
character: Logistics-and-landfill edge along the West Shore Expressway where Amazon warehouses and the Freshkills Park transformation are slowly converting industrial land into a demand center.

name: Bayside–Northeast Queens
character: Affluent suburban-form northeast Queens organized around Bell Boulevard dining, LIRR Port Washington stations and top-drawer schools.

name: Tribeca–SoHo
character: Affluent loft residential alongside a global flagship-shopping grid whose weekend foot traffic dwarfs its local population.

name: McKinney–Historic Downtown
character: The metro's best-preserved historic square as the living room of one of America's fastest-growing family suburbs, with destination weekend dining on Tennessee and Virginia.

name: Deep Ellum
character: Music-and-murals entertainment grid on the Elm and Commerce spines, running the metro's latest nights over a converting warehouse stock.

name: The Colony–Grandscape
character: 121 mega-retail node built around Nebraska Furniture Mart's Grandscape, pulling metro-wide weekend traffic over a lakeside golf-community residential base.

name: Little Elm
character: Lakeside boomtown whose new rooftops outrun the road network, with the city-built Lakefront district as its social anchor.

name: South Dallas–Martin Luther King
character: The historic Black main street of Dallas on the MLK spine, with freedmen's-town roots at Joppa, strong church-and-community institutions and thin national-brand supply.

name: East Fort Worth–Woodhaven
character: Stable working-family east-side grid running from Texas Wesleyan to the Woodhaven edge at the Arlington line, with the Eastchase power center as its retail anchor.

name: Keller–Old Town Keller
character: Affluent small-town suburb whose Old Town main street and top-rated schools anchor family dining and indie retail inside a chain strip landscape.

name: Burleson–Old Town
character: Fast-growing southwest family suburb where Old Town's heritage square anchors identity while new rooftops spread along SH-174 and I-35W.

name: Lakewood–Casa Linda
character: Affluent eastside neighborhoods orbiting two legacy retail plazas on the east side of White Rock Lake.

name: West Fort Worth–White Settlement
character: Working westside value belt on Camp Bowie West and White Settlement Road, anchored by the Lockheed Martin plant and the NAS JRB military payroll.

name: Downtown Fort Worth–Sundance Square
character: Sundance Square's managed plaza blocks and office towers below the Tarrant County courthouse bluff, mixing weekday workers with heritage tourists on Tarrant's most walkable grid.

name: Pleasant Grove
character: Working southeast Dallas family belt on Lake June and Buckner, where chain QSR coverage far outruns cafe, fitness and fast-casual supply.

name: Denton–Historic Square
character: Two-university county-seat square where UNT's music-school energy runs an indie coffee-and-bar grid around the 1896 courthouse.

name: Coppell–Old Coppell
character: Affluent family suburb wrapped around Old Town's small historic node, hemmed by freeway and airport edges at the metro's north logistics flank.

name: Plano–Legacy West
character: Corporate-campus premium mixed-use anchored by the Toyota NA and Liberty Mutual hosts, where Legacy West's luxury retail ring feeds on the office-day lunch and expense-account evening.

name: Irving–Old Irving
character: Working suburb around Old Irving's heritage core, with immigrant retail along Irving Boulevard and Belt Line and a TRE rail edge.

name: Design District–Trinity Groves
character: Showroom-and-studio zone along Dragon and Slocum with the Trinity Groves restaurant incubator as a special-zone overlay on its river edge.

name: Addison–Beltline
character: The metro's densest restaurant row on Belt Line Road over a corporate village grid, with Addison Circle and Vitruvian Park as its walkable pockets.

name: Rowlett–Downtown
character: Lakeside family suburb rebuilding a small downtown around the DART terminus while the Sapphire Bay lakefront project adds a destination edge.

name: West 7th–Montgomery Plaza
character: The metro's second late-night district on a converted department-store strip, running bar-and-patio volume between downtown and the museums.

name: Farmers Branch–Valwood
character: Warehouse-and-office belt repositioning toward mixed use around Brookhaven and the coming Silver Line station.

name: Arlington Entertainment District
character: Stadium-arena-theme-park cluster on the I-30 spine with a hotel strip and Texas Live! as the year-round dining floor; AT&T Stadium, Globe Life Field and Six Flags surges are special-zone overlays.

name: West Dallas–Trinity Corridor
character: Redevelopment frontier across the river from downtown, with new mixed-use nodes landing over longtime working Latino neighborhoods.

name: Benbrook
character: Quiet lake-edge suburb running family routines on US-377 and Bryant Irvin, with weekend demand tied to Benbrook Lake recreation.

name: Love Field–UTSW Medical
character: Airport edge wrapped around the UTSW–Parkland–Children's medical row, a 24-hour institutional demand engine whose hospital segments are scored later.

name: Alliance Town Center–Presidio
character: Master-planned corporate-and-retail boomtown on the I-35W flank of Texas Motor Speedway, where new rooftops keep arriving ahead of supply; race weekends are a special-zone overlay.

name: Richardson–Telecom Corridor
character: Telecom-era office spine on US-75 reborn around CityLine's rail-served mixed use, with UT Dallas pulling the north end younger.

name: Fair Park–South Dallas
character: Working residential grid wrapped around the Art Deco fairgrounds, where the State Fair surge is a special-zone overlay, not the corridor's baseline.

name: North Fort Worth–Saginaw
character: Established northside family grid around Saginaw and the I-35W/820 interchange, running on school-and-commute rhythms with value retail.

name: Bishop Arts District
character: Indie dining village in North Oak Cliff, largely arrived, pulling metro-wide weekend diners onto a two-block main-street grid.

name: Downtown Arlington–UTA
character: Historic Center Street main street and the College Park district riding a student-driven revival beside UTA's big commuter campus; the campus is a special-zone overlay.

name: Mesquite–Town East
character: East-metro chain retail anchored on the Town East mall special zone, with rodeo-arena heritage and a working, increasingly Hispanic residential grid.

name: Near Southside–Magnolia
character: Indie restaurant row and mural district on the Magnolia spine, anchored by the hospital cluster and Fairmount's historic housing stock.

name: Lewisville–Old Town
character: Established I-35E suburb whose revived Old Town main street and lake edge anchor a working, steadily diversifying retail base.

name: Carrollton–Old Downtown
character: Diverse established suburb where a Korean-anchored retail belt along Old Denton Road feeds a reviving rail-side historic square.

name: Lake Highlands
character: Established family grid of ranches and rebuilds feeding the Skillman–Audelia retail nodes near White Rock Lake.

name: Fort Worth Stockyards
character: Cattle-heritage tourism engine converting a working stockyard district into a full visitor product, with honky-tonk nightlife after dark.

name: North Dallas–Preston Hollow
character: Estate affluence and mature strip retail along Preston Road, with the Medical City hospital campus anchoring the northeast edge as a special-zone overlay.

name: Highland Park–University Park
character: Enclave wealth with its own police and school district, anchored by Highland Park Village and Snider Plaza, with NorthPark Center and SMU as hosted special zones on the edges.

name: Fort Worth South–Hemphill
character: Working Latino-first retail on the Hemphill arterial with the JPS hospital campus and corporate HQ anchors, serving its own neighborhoods more than visitors.

name: Cultural District–Museums
character: World-class museum campus and the Will Rogers event grounds with Dickies Arena surges as a special-zone overlay, ringed by leafy established neighborhoods.

name: Ridgmar–Lake Worth
character: Fading enclosed-mall node on I-30 giving way to big-box and lake-community retail along TX-199 toward Lake Worth.

name: Downtown Dallas–Main Street
character: The regional office core on DART's central rail junction, with converting towers and a growing but still thin after-hours residential base.

name: Allen–Watters Creek
character: Family suburb riding the US-75 retail belt, where Allen Premium Outlets and Watters Creek pull countywide weekend shoppers over a maturing subdivision grid.

name: Central Frisco–Downtown Frisco
character: Family boomtown's retail heart on the Stonebriar mall belt and Frisco Square civic node, with a small historic Rail District core holding Main Street.

name: Oak Lawn–Cedar Springs
character: LGBTQ main street on Cedar Springs with dense rentals and established dining, holding steady between Uptown's towers and the medical district.

name: Central Plano–Downtown Plano
character: Established suburb core with the heritage Downtown Plano square and the Red Line's Downtown Plano station, running on family routines and a maturing indie dining strip.

name: Grapevine–Historic Main
character: Wine-and-heritage Main Street holding indie tasting rooms and festival demand, with the Grapevine Mills outlet zone as a special-zone overlay rather than baseline.

name: Rockwall–Harbor
character: Affluent lakefront suburb: premium Harbor waterfront dining and a small historic square on Lake Ray Hubbard's east shore, gated by the I-30 causeway.

name: Far North Dallas
character: Tollway-corridor garden apartments and 1980s retail pads between LBJ and the George Bush Turnpike, running on commuter traffic.

name: Hurst–Euless–Bedford
character: Established mid-cities family belt of three towns along the 183 and 121 corridors, anchored by mall retail and a TRE station edge.

name: Las Colinas–Irving
character: Master-planned corporate district of office towers and the Mandalay Canal, running on a weekday office pulse with the Toyota Music Factory as its evening node.

name: Prosper–Celina
character: Master-planned boomtown frontier on the 380 corridor, where Windsong Ranch, Light Farms and the Gates of Prosper are landing rooftops faster than quality retail can follow.

name: DFW Airport–International Parkway
character: Hotel row and air-cargo logistics wrapped around the DFW Airport special zone; terminal demand belongs to the host, not scored into this corridor.

name: Uptown–Victory Park
character: Dense young-professional towers along the McKinney Avenue spine, with American Airlines Center event surges in Victory Park as a special-zone overlay.

name: Haltom City–North Richland Hills
character: Established postwar mid-north suburbs between the Airport Freeway and 820, mixing North Richland Hills' kept-up family subdivisions with Haltom City's value retail rows.

name: Flower Mound–Parker Square
character: High-income family suburb with top-tier safety whose retail gathers at Parker Square and the lake-edge Lakeside district along FM 2499.

name: Balch Springs–Seagoville
character: Working southeast fringe along the 175 spine: value retail, under-served rooftops and semi-rural edges toward Seagoville's old main street.

name: Galleria–Midtown
character: Mall-anchored hotel and retail node at the 635–tollway interchange, with the Valley View site mid-reinvention as Dallas Midtown.

name: Cedar Hill–Uptown Village
character: Escarpment-edge hill suburb where the Uptown Village lifestyle node serves family households above Joe Pool Lake and the state-park trail base.

name: Duncanville
character: Established first-ring southern suburb holding steady on a Main Street spine with big-box freeway edges and strong civic identity per capita.

name: Wylie–Sachse
character: Northeast Collin family belt on the SH-78 and Bush Turnpike edges, growing fast from working subdivisions toward the Lavon Lake shore.

name: Mansfield
character: Fast-growing family suburb on the US 287 spine, with a small historic main street and master-planned edges still pushing south into Johnson County prairie.

name: Grand Prairie
character: Working family suburb straddling the Dallas–Tarrant county line, with outlet, lakeside and Asian-market retail pulling regional weekend traffic.

name: Frisco–The Star
character: Boomtown's corporate-sports node at The Star and Toyota Stadium, with HALL Park and Frisco Station offices feeding a controlled-host retail ring.

name: TCU–Bluebonnet
character: Private-campus village on Berry Street and Bluebonnet Circle, ringed by established pre-war neighborhoods; game-day surges are a campus-zone overlay, not the baseline.

name: East Dallas–Gaston
character: Baylor hospital's employment engine on a working eastside retail spine, with historic-district infill edging in from Peak's Addition and Junius Heights.

name: Oak Cliff–Jefferson
character: Latino-first shopping spine where quinceanera retail and taquerias outdraw the chains, with Bishop Arts' indie halo pushing east along the boulevard.

name: Forest Hill–Everman
character: Working south-Tarrant pair of small cities along I-35W and SE Loop 820, with value retail serving its own rooftops and little through-draw.

name: DeSoto–Lancaster
character: Established Black middle-class family suburbs on the I-35E spine, with two small heritage squares holding local identity beneath the chain frontage.

name: Southlake–Colleyville
character: Executive-family suburbs anchored by Southlake Town Square's curated retail and the Westlake corporate campuses along 114.

name: Garland–Downtown Garland
character: Large first-ring working suburb: an indie-leaning historic square and DART Blue Line edge against chain-dominated arterials and Firewheel lifestyle retail.
